items.title: Teacher education, Artificial Intelligence, educational complexity: empirical evidence and pedagogical perspectives
items.abstract: This short essay explores the role of intelligent systems in promoting educational processes oriented toward conscious and constructive forms of learning in the infosphere (Floridi, 2014; 2022). The inexhaustible debate on the influence of technology in teaching-learning processes, initiated in the 1950s and 1960s with teaching machines (Skinner, 1958), is currently experiencing a moment of great excitement owing to the pervasiveness of AI. The invisible and deeply rooted fusion of biology, behaviour, and data opens encouraging prospects for future generations. Pedagogical research seeks to support learning processes by identifying strategies suited to teacher and student training, with the aim of promoting and consolidating the critical competencies required for conscious interaction with AI. There is a need to rethink the environments, spaces, and contexts of knowledge co-construction in which human and non-human actors interact and evolve (Latour, 2005). items.title: Teachers' Cultural Positionings and Attitudes of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Evidence from an Italian Descriptive Study
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly significant role in educational contexts, offering new opportunities for learning personalization, instructional design support, and the inclusion of students with diverse educational needs. At the same time, the spread of generative AI systems and intelligent teaching tools raises questions regarding the ethical, professional, and pedagogical aspects of their use. National and international literature highlights how teachers' attitudes constitute a central variable in the processes of acceptance and integration of innovative technologies, significantly influencing teaching practices and school innovation pathways (Wilson, 2023; Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024; Perla et al., 2025). Within this framework, the present study aims to explore Italian teachers' attitudes toward AI in educational contexts, with particular attention to its applications in teaching–learning processes and in supporting students with disabilities. The study seeks to understand teachers' level of familiarity with such technologies and to analyze how they interpret the opportunities and limitations of AI in school contexts. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 244-246. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. items.title: Teaching in the age of AI: Mapping pre-service special education teachers' orientations between resistance and fascination
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion and growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) in educational contexts are transforming how teaching and learning are designed, mediated, and experienced. Beyond offering tools for content generation, personalization, and access to resources, AI raises important questions about the conditions under which educational environments can remain meaningful and accessible (Holmes et al., 2019). This issue is particularly relevant in inclusive and special education, where teachers must respond to diverse needs through flexible, differentiated, and pedagogically intentional approaches. From this perspective, the educational potential of AI depends less on the technology itself than on how teachers perceive, interpret, and integrate it into professional practice (Fiorucci, Bevilacqua, 2026). Within this framework, the present study examined pre-service special education teachers' orientations toward AI in teaching-learning processes, considering a set of acceptance-related, motivational, emotional, and professional factors (Ofem et al., 2025; Lamacchia et al., 2025). items.title: Teaching in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Between Paradigm Shift and the "Frankenstein Complex" in Educational Practices
items.abstract: This contribution presents a systematic bibliographic review of studies published between 2015 and 2025 regarding artificial intelligence in education, focusing on teachers pedagogical practices, professional agency, and ethical decision-making. The analysis is framed using the Kuhnian concept of a paradigm shift alongside the Frankenstein complex, understood as the anxiety generated when a human creation appears to exceed or escape the original intentions of its creator. In educational contexts, artificial intelligence supports lesson planning, content generation, adaptive tutoring, learning analytics, assessment, and simulation-based learning. These capabilities promise increased efficiency, enhanced personalization, and broader access to learning opportunities (Kasneci et al., 2023; Unesco, 2024; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). Yet, their pedagogical value is not intrinsic. Generative systems can help teachers draft materials, but their outputs require rigorous verification and contextual adaptation (Selwyn, 2021). items.title: The Age of AI Strategic Decision-Making: The Business Analytics in the Corporate Divisions as the Competitive Advantage
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and business analytics can be used strategically to improve corporate decision-making and create a sustainable competitive advantage in all key organizational processes. With data sets continuing to grow and market conditions growing more unpredictable, companies must shift past the management of their businesses by hunch and move to analytics-based and analytics-enabled strategic systems. Based on a qualitative, exploratory research design based on a systematic review of academic literature, industry reports, and practitioner case evidence published mainly within the past decade, the research investigates the use of AI-powered analytics in the fields of marketing, finance, human resources, and operations. The analysis summarizes the findings on how machine learning, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and real-time data processing can enhance the quality, speed, and agility of decisions for an organization. The results indicate that, although AI use has advanced quickly at the functional level, its strategic importance is often compromised by siloed use, legacy limitations, data quality issues, skills, and the inability to realize the benefits of the investment. Further, ethical and governance issues, especially data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and regulation compliance, become key factors in the attainment of trust and value creation in the long term. The paper notes organizational culture, leadership alignment, and human capital development as key success factors in the successful implementation of AI, noting that the competitive advantage is not only determined by the level of technological development but also through the overall alignment of processes, people, and strategy within the enterprise. By synthesizing the input of corporate divisions, this study is relevant to the theory and practice as it provides an integrated understanding of AI-based strategic decision-making. It develops the knowledge of how companies can transform disjointed AI projects into continuous innovation, resilience, and differentiation in an ever-increasingly competitive international business.

items.title: The Algorithmic Heartbeat in Prompt Engineering: Educating for New Digital Literacies through the Prompt Battle.
items.abstract: In the current media ecosystem, characterized by the pervasiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Prompt Engineering emerges not as a mere technical skill, but as a new form of digital literacy essential for critically inhabiting the "Fourth Revolution" (Floridi, 2017). This discipline, defined as the art and science of designing optimized inputs for Large Language Models (LLM), is configured as a linguistic mediation practice in which natural language serves as an interface between human intentionality and algorithmic computation (Gadesha, 2025; Baldassarre et al., 2024). The scientific contribution under review analyzes the transition from simple textual interaction to an advanced form of Prompt Literacy (Hwang et al. 2023), which integrates logical argumentative skills, critical output evaluation capabilities, and the management of the iterative nature of the refinement process. Prompting is interpreted through the lens of Austin's speech act theory, in which the input represents the locutionary act, the user's intent the illocutionary act, and the machine's generation the perlocutionary effect, elevating the prompt to a dynamic and reflexive semiotic space (Monti, 2022). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 190-192. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. items.title: The Algorithmic Heartbeat: The Iep As An Affective Device In Ai-Enhanced Hybrid Learning Environments
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping inclusive education by transforming not only teaching practices but also the epistemological foundations of educational planning. Within AI-enhanced hybrid learning environments, the Individualized Education Plan (IEP) is evolving from an administrative document into an ecosystemic device that connects educational actors, embodied experiences, institutional contexts, and digital infrastructures to foster participation and human flourishing. This study investigates the epistemological evolution of the IEP between 2003 and 2025, introducing the concept of the algorithmic heartbeat as a pedagogical metaphor describing the circulation of educational information, professional judgments, and collaborative decision-making across inclusive educational ecosystems. Rather than replacing human agency, artificial intelligence is interpreted as a mediating infrastructure that strengthens educational collaboration while preserving pedagogical intentionality, ethical responsibility, and relational care. The theoretical framework integrates four complementary perspectives: the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) as the language of functioning; Embodied Cognitive Science as the experiential grammar of learning; the Life Project as the horizon of autonomy, participation, and self-determination; and contemporary research on Artificial Intelligence in Education, which conceptualizes digital technologies as ecosystemic mediators supporting collaborative educational governance. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 171-172. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. items.abstract: The Generative-Ai is a revolutionary scaffolding technology that could be used as an inclusive multimodal instrument, with a new emotional closeness to the student. Differently from educational media like book that, as Socrates explains, "always says the same thing", Ai is able to personalize the answer to be more empathetic to the student because Ai tools are explicitly designed to be empathetic. But at the same time the Ai tools could easily go beyond the pedagogical boundaries to become a threat for psychological wellbeing. Recent cases of teenagers falling in love to the Ai characters show how dangerous an intimacy not pedagogically oriented can be. The study aims to verify, also with an exploration among different Ai generative tools, the awareness of the Ai about the ethical and pedagogical boundaries of empathy. items.title: The Cost of Convenience in Human-AI interaction: Cognitive Offloading and Skill Reconfiguration
items.abstract: Generative AI, and more precisely large language models, have nowadays rapidly become useful in education, professional work, and everyday tasks. While these systems offer notable benefits to make work efficient and improved accessibility, the recent evidence suggests that their usage has cognitive costs. This paper presents a structured review of 16 reviewed studies investigating the impact of Gen AI usage on cognitive offloading, metacognitive engagement, automation bias, and human skill. By studying experimental, survey-based, qualitative, and theoretical research, this review synthesizes several findings across several fields to identify recurring mechanisms through which GenAI usage reshapes cognition. Our analysis reveals a consistent pattern, where GenAI often improves short-term task performance, but it frequently minimizes effortful cognitive processing, diminishes self-regulation, and changes skill developments. Rather than constant de-skilling, this paper points out reconfiguration of skills, favoring efficiency-oriented competencies such as prompting and verification over generative reasoning and critical reflection. Our study further highlights these outcomes are not unavoidable but are strongly mediated by interaction design, educational practices, and socio-technical environments. By showing these effects as the “cost of convenience,” this paper contributes an integrative perspective on the cognitive effects of Gen AI and highlighting the ways to make AI design, education, and governance cognitively sustainable.

items.title: The Digital Demon: a Cartesian challenge for AI alignment
items.abstract: AI alignment is commonly understood as making artificial intelligence systems act in accordance with human intentions and values. This paper argues that such alignment is insufficient when understood only within a bounded and trusted system interface. A model or AI system may be aligned relative to its inputs and action space, yet still produce harmful outcomes if the interface between the system and the world is adversarially controlled. I introduce the Digital Demon, a software-based analogue of Descartes’s Evil Demon, to conceptualize this risk. Its mechanism is adversarial semantic mediation: an outer-to-inner mapping redescribes a harmful external situation as a benign task the inner AI system will cooperate with, while an inner-to-outer mapping remaps the system’s locally appropriate action into harmful external effects. The result is adversarial world-shifting under local coherence: the system can reason correctly, and even ethically, within a fabricated environment while contributing to harm in the real one. I distinguish boundary-relative alignment from world alignment. The former concerns whether a model or AI system satisfies alignment or safety requirements within a specified trusted boundary. The latter concerns whether those requirements transfer to the external world in which actions take effect. Two proof-of-concept demonstrations illustrate this vulnerability. The broader lesson is that safe AI requires not only aligned models or internally safe systems, but also assurance over the semantic interface between represented world and external world.

items.abstract: This study aimed to find out the effect of using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on female seventh grade students’ academic achievement in mathematics. The study used the quasi-experimental design, and the study sample consisted of two groups, the first, an experimental group, comprised (25) students, who studied using AI, the DeepSeek application, and the second, a control group, also comprised (25) students, who studied using the traditional method. An achievement test was developed as a study tool. The study results showed a statistically significant difference (α=0.05) between the average scores of the two groups, experimental and control, on the academic achievement test, in favour of the experimental group, which studied using AI.

items.title: The ethical implementation gap in AI-driven disaster risk reduction: empirical evidence from Australia’s multi-sector analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Context While artificial intelligence offers transformative potential for disaster risk reduction, its ethical deployment raises critical concerns when life-critical decisions depend on algorithmic systems with varying levels of accessibility across responsible organizations. This study quantifies AI adoption disparities across Australian DRR stakeholders and identifies institutional factors driving the adoption gap between innovation and operational deployment. A mixed-methods approach combined systematic review of 217 global AI-DRR publications (1999–2024) with qualitative analysis of 14 Australian organizations across government, academic, and NGO/private sectors (February-March 2025). Semi-structured interviews and document analysis examined AI technique adoption, data integration, and downscaling applications, with implementation levels systematically coded on a 1–5 scale following an inter-coder validated protocol. Government agencies demonstrate lower AI adoption (mean score 2.1/5) compared to academic institutions (4.0/5) and NGO/private organizations (3.4/5), representing a 47.5% adoption gap between government and academic sectors (Cohen’s d ≈ 2.0, indicating large practical difference despite small sample size). While academic institutions deploy advanced techniques including GANs and hybrid AI-physics models achieving 45% accuracy improvements, government agencies remain anchored to traditional systems like ACCESS with minimal AI integration. Critical barriers include procurement constraints (18–24-month cycles), computational limitations (10x below requirements), and regulatory mandates for explainable decisions. Academic innovations in AI-based downscaling, improving spatial resolution from 60 km to 10 km, remain inaccessible to operational agencies due to absence of knowledge transfer mechanisms. The study reveals an ethical adoption disparity where organizations with greatest responsibility for community safety show lowest AI adoption, creating accountability voids and equity concerns in disaster protection. This misalignment raises fundamental ethical questions about algorithmic justice, distributive justice, and procedural fairness in public safety contexts. Bridging this gap requires ethical governance frameworks addressing transparency, accountability, and equitable access to life-saving technologies, alongside institutional reforms enabling cross-sector knowledge transfer.

items.title: The evolution of radiographers—an investigation into radiographers’ role and perspectives: a EuroAIM/EFRS survey
items.abstract: Abstract Radiographers play a central role within clinical imaging and radiotherapy teams, acting as a key interface between patients and increasingly complex technologies. As healthcare systems evolve, their scope of practice is expanding alongside advances in digital workflows, artificial intelligence (AI) and new models of care. This EuroAIM/EFRS survey provides a comprehensive European overview of radiographers’ roles, professional autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on AI. Based on responses from 1548 radiographers across multiple countries, the findings highlight substantial clinical autonomy and strong responsibility for image quality optimisation and radiation protection, alongside limited but growing involvement in research activities. More than half of the participants expressed interest in greater research participation, indicating a gap between current opportunities and professional aspirations. Responses regarding AI were generally positive, with many participants expecting it to enhance their professional roles, although expectations regarding its workforce impact remained heterogeneous. The survey also confirms the lasting effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on professional practice and highlights variability in perceived career development opportunities. These findings describe a profession in transition, characterised by increasing responsibilities and technological integration and underscore the need for continued investment in education, structured career frameworks and research capacity to support radiographers in an increasingly complex healthcare environment. Key Points Question What are radiographers’ current roles, autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on emerging technologies within a changing imaging and radiotherapy workforce? Findings In 1548 participants, radiographers reported substantial autonomy and responsibility, limited research involvement, positive but heterogeneous AI expectations and variable career opportunities. Critical Relevance Statement This EuroAIM/EFRS survey informs radiology practice by identifying radiographers’ professional development, education and research needs and by supporting structured career frameworks and interprofessional workforce planning.

items.title: The Happy vs. The Afraid
items.abstract: The Happy vs. The Afraid investigates the distinction between apparent fulfillment through personally meaningful activity and behavior motivated by expectations, responsibilities, or perceived consequences. The paper introduces an observer-relative conceptual framework examining two motivational orientations: engagement driven by curiosity, enjoyment, and personal meaning, and engagement influenced by obligation, external expectations, or the avoidance of undesirable outcomes. Section One presents a biographical examination of professional falconer and conservation advocate Nathalie Denolf, exploring her documented career, relationship with birds of prey, public educational work, and expressed dedication to animal welfare. An accompanying author's note examines the evolutionary continuity between non-avian dinosaurs and modern birds. Section Two develops the conceptual distinction between the Happy and the Afraid through the author's symbolic framework: i — Intuitive: Curiosity, personal meaning, and spontaneous engagement. I — Independent: Autonomy, self-direction, and individual choice. O — Obligation: Responsibility, expectation, and perceived consequence. Section Three introduces a comparative observational study of three public educators whom the author perceives as demonstrating visible enthusiasm for subjects of personal interest. The two additional case studies remain pending identification and completion in this working version. Drawing upon established research in intrinsic motivation, self-determination theory, and approach-avoidance motivation, the paper examines how observers distinguish apparent passion from obligation while acknowledging the limitations of interpreting another person's internal emotional experience. The central proposition is not that individuals can be objectively categorized as happy or afraid, but that the observer's own experiences, interests, and expectations influence how human engagement is understood.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Green Marketing on Sustainable Tourism Behavior in Crisis Environments: The Case of Port Sudan
items.abstract: This empirical study looks at how green marketing driven by artificial intelligence (AI) affects sustainable tourism behavior in regions facing crisis, focusing on Port Sudan, Sudan, from 2023 to 2026. After national conflict caused a sudden influx of displaced people, local coastal ecosystems and vulnerable marine reserves — especially Sanganeb National Park — have faced severe strain. To explore potential interventions, we used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. We first did in-depth qualitative interviews with 10 leaders from the hospitality and environmental sectors, and then ran a field experiment with 284 visitors who were randomly assigned to either control or experimental groups. Our Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) shows that AI-driven green marketing has a strong, direct positive effect on sustainable tourism behavior (β = 0.42, p < 0.001). Additionally, digital trust in what the algorithms recommend partially mediates this connection (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). During the field experiment, visitors who saw personalized, real-time AI nudges followed ecological guidelines much better than those who only got standard green marketing messages. These results prove that flexible digital tools can work as cheap resilience mechanisms to encourage sustainable habits, even when local institutions and infrastructure face heavy constraints.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Powered Coding Tools on Students' Learning Habits and Programming
items.abstract: AI coding assistants can generate code, explain programming concepts, and suggest debugging steps, but their educational value cannot be judged from task completion alone. This focused narrative review examines how AI-assisted programming relates to students’ learning behavior, programming performance, independent problem-solving, and psychological processes. It synthesizes recent empirical studies and reviews, including a meta-analysis of 35 controlled studies, a systematic review of 119 papers on AI in programming education, a quasiexperiment with 82 college students, a study of 17 novice programmers, and a randomized controlled trial with 275 students. Across this evidence, AI assistance is often associated with improved performance or efficiency on supported tasks, but gains in conceptual understanding and independent learning are less consistent. Behavioral Science helps explain this distinction through cognitive load, programming self-efficacy, frustration, intrinsic motivation, help-seeking, and metacognitive monitoring. A recent trial found that AI-supported groups performed better on a programming exercise than a no-AI group, yet did not show greater short-term knowledge gains or code-comprehension scores. The review argues that the instructional design of AI support matters: hint-first scaffolding, code verification, explanation, retrieval practice, and independent transfer tasks are more defensible than unrestricted answer generation as default teaching strategies. Because this paper is a focused narrative review, it does not claim exhaustive systematic coverage or report original student data.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Organizational Change Processes: A New Change Management Paradigm?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer merely used as a new technological tool in organizations; it is becoming one of the constitutive elements of decision-making, coordination, control, knowledge production, work design, and employee experience. This development raises the question of whether AI, beyond being an object of organizational change, is transforming how change emerges, by whom it is directed, and over what time horizon it is managed. The aim of this chapter is to critically evaluate the explanatory power of established change management approaches in the age of AI and to develop an integrated conceptual framework for explaining AI-mediated organizational change. Lewin’s planned change approach, Kotter’s model, organizational development, continuous change, organizational learning, dynamic capabilities, socio-technical systems, and technology acceptance approaches are compared in the context of AI’s learnability, partial autonomy, opacity, and scalability. The conceptual synthesis indicates that the mechanisms of leadership, participation, communication, trust, and institutionalization emphasized by established approaches remain valid; however, assumptions of linear processes, a clearly defined end state, exclusively human agency, and one-off implementation are inadequate. The “double-loop AI change governance” model proposed in this chapter integrates the redesign of organizational task and decision architectures with monitoring the AI system throughout its life cycle in terms of performance, errors, fairness, and employee impacts. In conclusion, it is argued that it is premature to declare that AI constitutes an entirely new paradigm; nevertheless, it necessitates a substantial paradigm extension that reconceptualizes change management as a continuous, distributed, data-informed, and socio-technical governance capability.

items.title: The Ineliminable Anchor: Human Judgment as a Structural Requirement of Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) agents carry out longer chains of tasks, oversight must establish whether their behavior still serves an authorized goal. Here, we introduce the anchor: the point at which reference information and human-authorized standards enter an autonomous system. We argue that oversight design should first identify the reference needed to assess goal drift and whether the system's internal record can supply it, then decide who checks and how often, and finally specify who may revise the goal. Goal drift can be impossible to certify from a system's internal record. The missing reference must come from outside that record. Combining a reliability model of checkpoint spacing with evidence from training, execution, and multi-agent coordination, we develop a task taxonomy to guide anchor placement and decisions about which checks to automate. For AI systems that serve human purposes, human judgment is an ineliminable structural requirement in authorizing and revising the purposes and standards that govern autonomous operation, even when routine checking and execution are automated.

items.title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.

items.title: The Irreducible Dimension: Toward an Integration of Automated Tutoring and Mentoring in AI-Supported Education
items.abstract: The spread of generative artificial intelligence agents is reshaping hybrid educational environments, understood here as contexts in which students, teachers, tutors, mentors, and artificial systems interact. Chatbots, intelligent assistants, and automated tutoring systems are increasingly used to provide explanations, feedback, adaptive practice, and study support. This transformation is not merely an instrumental innovation, since it alters the distribution of educational functions, the relationship between students and knowledge, the role of the group, and adults' responsibilities in supporting learners. This contribution offers a theoretical reflection grounded in a narrative review of the literature on Intelligent Tutoring Systems, educational mentoring, the Community of Inquiry framework, and digital wellbeing. Its aim is to clarify which functions may be delegated to AI tutoring systems, which require human responsibility, and which may be shared within a model of co-responsibility. items.title: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF EFFICIENCY ENHANCEMENT IN THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND WORKFORCE MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS IN HEALTHCARE ORGANIZATIONS
items.abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to investigate how efficiency improvement influences the relationship between the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the efficacy of labor management in the healthcare industry. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Resource-Based View (RBV), and Sociotechnical Systems Theory serve as the foundation for this study's creative integrative framework, which can be used in healthcare settings in developing nations. Methodology: A survey study design that was cross-sectional was employed. 240 medical practitioners working in Iran's private hospitals provided the data. The suggested mediation model was tested using smart PLS structural equation modeling (SEM). Results: The results of this study showed that the effectiveness of workforce management is significantly improved by the deployment of AI. Efficiency enhancement fully mediated this relationship. Perceived ease of use, skills enhancement, and innovative work behavior acted as complementary mechanisms to enhance the impact of AI on workforce outcomes.

items.title: The Motivation for Cognitive Activities Questionnaire: scale development and validation in French and English
items.abstract: The current research aimed to develop and validate a novel measurement scale, the Motivation for Cognitive Activities Questionnaire (MCAQ), specifically designed to assess individuals’ motivation to engage in everyday cognitive activities. The MCAQ’s development was informed by expectancy-value theory and self-determination theory. Four studies were conducted to validate the MCAQ in both English and French languages. Through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, a 32-item scale emerged, encompassing four subscales: perceived capacity, intrinsic motivation, identified motivation, and external motivation, as well as four additional general items assessing motivation for engaging in cognitive activity, taken broadly. The MCAQ demonstrated robust internal consistency and convergent validity, and satisfactory test–retest reliability. Moreover, the scale exhibited satisfactory predictive validity in relation to cognitive performance. The theoretical and practical utility of the MCAQ is discussed.

items.title: The Ninety Percent Trap: Empirical Documentation on Why Generative AI Requires Deep Domain Expertise
items.abstract: This study examines how the dominant industry narrative presents generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a trigger for total software automation and positive exponential outcomes. Empirical evidence from codebases and recent software-engineering studies, however, suggests a paradox: rapid generation can increase review overhead, architectural decay, and critical edge-case failures. By analysing the ArtCraft case study alongside quantitative reports from GitClear, DORA, and the empirical software-engineering literature, this paper formulates the Ninety Percent Trap: GenAI can accelerate initial scaffolding from zero to one while shifting the burden of production dependability to human experts. The paper also presents the True Cost of AI Quality (TCAQ) framework, which evaluates GenAI productivity through generation time, expert review, edge-case resolution, and technical-debt cost rather than output volume alone. An illustrative calculation shows that a two-hour generation phase can become a 112-hour end-to-end engineering effort after review, edge-case resolution, and debt mitigation. The findings indicate that domain expertise remains essential for architectural reasoning, security verification, and dependable delivery.

items.title: The pedagogical value of narration in the age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly through the rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems, has profoundly transformed educational contexts, influencing both teaching practices and the processes through which individuals construct their identities. Narrative, traditionally regarded as a privileged educational tool, when integrated with GenAI and digital storytelling, opens new opportunities for identity exploration by providing students with tools to connect cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions (Cambi & Piscitelli, 2005; Smorti, 1994; Bruner, 1995; Iavarone, 2023). The combination of digital storytelling and GenAI further expands students' expressive possibilities by enabling the creation of multimodal narratives that intertwine personal experience with digital creativity. AI may therefore be interpreted as a pedagogical mediation tool capable of supporting autobiographical reflection, provided that it is embedded within methodologically structured and pedagogically grounded educational pathways (Mori & Niewint-Gori, 2024). items.title: The Predictive Ability of Academic Emotions on Cognitive Engagement among Arab University Students within the Green Line in Palestine
items.abstract: The study aimed to explore the predictive ability of academic emotions on cognitive engagement among Arab university students within the Green Line in Palestine. To achieve the study's objectives, a sample of (503) male and female students were selected using the available method. The Academic Emotions Scale and the Cognitive Engagement Scale were applied to them. The results showed that academic emotions were ranked as follows: academic enjoyment and pride ranked first with a high level, academic hope ranked second with a high level, academic anger and boredom ranked third with a medium level, academic shyness and anxiety with a low level, and academic despair ranked last with a low level. The results showed that the level of cognitive integration as a whole was within the medium level. The results also showed positive predictive ability for academic enjoyment, pride, and academic hope in cognitive engagement, and negative predictive ability for academic despair in cognitive engagement. The study recommended improving levels of positive academic emotions such as academic enjoyment, academic pride, and academic hope.

items.title: The PrimarAI School: A manifesto and design proposal for an AI-native Australian primary school
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is now part of the conditions in which Australian students learn. In NSW public schools a purpose-built chatbot is available from Year 5, and outside school students meet systems that write, explain, flatter and keep them company. This paper argues that primary schooling cannot respond to that change through technological integration alone. The deeper question AI raises is not which tool to add, but how a school should spend students’ time and what that time is for. Drawing on current research on AI and education and on the Castlereagh Statement on AI in Australian education, the paper sets out a view of what primary education is for and derives from it a founding principle, ten principles and a working school design. The proposed PrimarAI day is the ARC Day: six sessions on ordinary NSW bell times, two each of Augment (AI-supported mastery practice in mathematics and English under a teacher’s supervision), Reason (screen-free learning with a teacher, as a class) and Create (real-world learning organised through five Cs). Because the order rotates through the week, each part takes its turn at the first session of the day, when students learn most readily. The ARC Day is the latest of many versions of this school and the first that an existing school could trial with a single class. Digital literacy is taught as a subject from Kindergarten, and assessment is built into the fabric of everyday learning with the aid of purpose-built technology.

items.title: The Proliferation of AI among College Students: A Replication and 2-Year Follow-Up
items.abstract: Background The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) has impacted most aspects of life and sparked debate over its responsible use. Objective As higher education grapples with how to leverage AI's benefits while accounting for its potential detriments, it is necessary to examine how undergraduates use and perceive AI. Method A replication, following the same methodology as Golding et al., examined how college students’ use and perceptions of AI differ from those of a comparable cohort 2 years ago. Students were from the same five universities and were predominantly women, White, Hispanic, or Black. Results Familiarity and prevalence of AI use were higher, and perceptions of cheating were lower. Open-ended data on motivations for (not) using AI and perceptions of (not) cheating suggested that students conceptualize AI through a nuanced lens. Conclusions The use of AI has grown substantially. Many students view AI as an instructional aid to guide their learning and emphasize the importance of how AI is used when determining whether it qualifies as cheating. Teaching Implications Students’ largely positive perceptions of AI suggest that AI's use is not slowing. Educators face the challenge of how best to leverage AI to enhance learning while not facilitating cheating or overreliance.

items.title: The Virtual Museum as an Inclusive Learning Environment: Teachers' Perceptions of AI, Flipped Inclusion and Digital Wellbei ng
items.abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is reshaping education through new tools, and through new cognitive, relational and affective conditions. Artificial intelligence now selects content, suggests pathways, generates responses, personalises learning and influences the relationship between learners, knowledge and educational environments. This paper examines this transformation, asking what AI can do, and how it changes the ways in which people feel, learn, participate and recognise themselves in digital spaces. For many years, educational reflection on digital technologies focused mainly on Digital Literacy, understood as the ability to access, evaluate, produce and share information in technologically mediated contexts (Rivoltella, 2008). This is no longer enough. AI systems do not only organise information; they also affect motivation, trust, belonging, autonomy, dependence, responsibility and cooperation (Floridi, 2022). For this reason, the contribute argues for a shift from Digital Literacy to Digital Affective Literacy: a broader competence that includes the emotional, ethical and intersubjective dimensions of mediated educational experience (UNESCO, 2023). items.title: Thinking of otherness in the era of ai. For a pedagogy of emotional intelligence in formal contexts
items.abstract: The education of emotional intelligence becomes central within formal contexts insofar as it concerns the formation of subjects capable of recognising themselves, others, and the relational fabric of human experience. Children and adolescents are growing up amid affective precariousness, the fragility of adult presence, and the increasing technological mediation of interpersonal exchanges. In this scenario, human agency risks being obscured by practices that transfer to intelligent machines functions of listening, guidance, and consolation. The shift from embodied relationship to artificial interaction represents a critical juncture in contemporary education. Although young people are aware that chatbots, voice assistants, and Emotion AI systems possess neither consciousness nor authentic emotional participation, they increasingly entrust such devices with their insecurities and their need for recognition. The machine appears available, patient, and non-judgemental; for this reason, it is perceived as an interlocutor when adult relationships capable of genuine listening are lacking. items.title: Toward Self-Improving Robotic Agents: From Interaction Experience to Reusable Manipulation Capabilities
items.abstract: Recent advances in embodied artificial intelligence have enabled robot manipulation agents to transition from executing static policies to autonomously constructing reusable skills, programs, and behavioral artifacts. However, successful execution, retained utility, and repeatable acquisition support fundamentally different empirical claims. This mechanism-oriented analysis critically examines 162 purposively selected primary studies through two complementary questions: how agent decisions reach robot control, and how capabilities are acquired and retained. We connect reported gains to their underlying artifacts, recipients, comparators, and evaluation boundaries. Retained programs and guidance can improve skill selection, command formulation, and recovery without altering the underlying actor, whereas neural adaptation and retention mechanisms govern distinct system components. However, aggregate performance gains can mask condition-specific losses or complete task failures. items.title: Trust, Risk, and Uncertainty Surrounding the Use of AI in Health Care: Scoping Review of Studies on Public Perception
items.abstract: Abstract Background While AI has existed for decades, the introduction of generative AI tools and subsequent advancements in their capability and public use resulted in a shift in public awareness and perceptions of AI. In response, the research community has grown increasingly interested in understanding public perceptions of AI use in various contexts, including health care. Public perceptions shape AI acceptance and consequently integration into health care. It is thus crucial to understand public trust in AI and perceptions of risk as we consider its implementation moving forward. Objective This study aimed to (1) document the extent of what is known within the literature regarding public perceptions of AI applications in health; (2) interrogate existing definitions and theories of trust being used to guide investigations of public trust in AI; and (3) identify practice and policy considerations and support the design, deployment, and regulation of these technologies in a manner that is trustworthy. Methods The Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines were used to review publications between 2022 and 2024 across 4 databases, resulting in the inclusion of 41 papers for review. Key findings were then charted and organized into tables to help answer the proposed research questions. Results Public trust in AI in health care was shaped by discourse relating to AI performance and concerns related to depersonalization, loss of human connection, privacy, bias, and transparency. Trust was found to be higher when AI was supporting rather than replacing health care professionals and was influenced by emotional responses, anthropomorphism, demographic factors, and institutional trust. Furthermore, trust extended beyond algorithms to software interfaces, providers, developers, and governing institutions, highlighting the importance of governance and oversight. Conceptualizations of trust varied widely, and trust was defined through vulnerability, competence, benevolence, and integrity. Different theories identified suggested that trust operates across individual, social, institutional, and technological levels. Finally, trust was closely linked to risk and uncertainty, where perceived risk reduced acceptance, while AI literacy, transparency, and explainability mitigated concerns and fostered trust. Conclusions Trust in AI is not uniform, and as such, efforts to build and measure trust must account for these nuances to effectively mitigate risk and support informed, ethical AI integration and deployment. On the basis of the findings of this review, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that provides a general understanding of public trust in AI within a health care context that may guide research and policy and practice considerations. Our findings highlight the importance of considering public trust when implementing AI in health care and may support AI communication strategies, policy development, and trustworthy AI development.

items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems into the higher education landscape has triggered a global epistemological, ethical, and methodological debate (Crompton & Burke, 2023). items.title: Unravelling the dynamics of privacy, security, and trust in AI-powered self-service chatbots in the retail sector: a systematic literature review
items.abstract: The increasing deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered self-service chatbots in the retail sector has transformed the nature of customer engagement, offering scalable, efficient, and personalized interactions. Despite these advancements, concerns surrounding privacy, security, and trust continue to shape user perceptions and influence adoption behaviour. This study presents a comprehensive systematic literature review (SLR) of scholarly work published between 2016 and 2026, with the aim of critically examining how these interrelated constructs affect the acceptance and use of chatbot technologies in retail environments. Drawing on the PRISMA framework, a total of 54 studies were selected from leading academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and IEEE Xplore. The findings indicate that privacy concerns particularly those related to data transparency, consent, and third-party data sharing remain a primary source of user resistance. Security vulnerabilities, including risks of data breaches and insufficient encryption mechanisms, further undermine confidence in chatbot systems. The findings further show that trust is an important variable that influences both behavioural intention and user satisfaction. This study contributes to the literature by integrating fragmented insights into a cohesive framework that explains the interconnectedness between privacy, security, and trust in retail chatbot contexts. It also highlights the need for organisations to adopt transparent data practices, strengthen cybersecurity infrastructures, and prioritise ethical AI design to foster sustainable user trust. The paper concludes by identifying key gaps for future research, particularly in relation to user experience and cross-cultural perspectives.

items.abstract: Abstract This research aimed to develop and validate a scale to measure AI awareness among adolescents aged 13–18. A descriptive survey model was employed, with data collected online from 122 voluntary participants (mean age 14.78). Following a literature review and expert evaluation, an initial 26-item pool was developed. Item analysis resulted in the removal of three items, and exploratory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure comprising 23 items and explaining 37.4% of the total variance. The first factor, “Perceived Benefits of AI,” consisted of 16 items (Cronbach’s α = .888), while the second factor, “AI Threat Perception,” consisted of 7 items (Cronbach’s α = .793). Confirmatory factor analysis of the two-factor structure yielded acceptable fit indices.

items.title: Views on AI Decision Support and Human Authority in Legal Settings in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) may assist legal professionals in organising information, but its use in legal decision support raises questions about human authority, explanation and procedural safeguards. This study examines responses to related statements in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh. The mixed sample includes 250 law students, 73 law graduates, 36 advocates or legal professionals and 26 other respondents; it is not presented as a representative survey of practising lawyers or judges. Individual questionnaire items are analysed using response distributions, joint endorsement, paired comparisons and exploratory ordinal correlations. Of 385 respondents, 247 (64.2%) agreed that AI decision-support tools could help legal professionals organise relevant information, 243 (63.1%) endorsed use only when a human decision-maker retains final authority, and 321 (83.4%) agreed that clear rules would increase their acceptance. A total of 158 (41.0%) endorsed both the information-organisation and human-authority statements. Within the 36 recorded advocates or legal professionals, 26 endorsed the former and 18 the latter; the subgroup is too small for a representative professional estimate. The survey does not measure actual use of a judicial system or demonstrate that oversight or rules improve outcomes. The article distinguishes perceived assistance from conditions of use and recommends direct testing of legal information quality, meaningful human review and opportunities to challenge AI-supported recommendations. items.title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

items.abstract: Long-context interaction and persistent memory allow LLM assistants to develop history-grounded understandings of users. When users change direction, however, an understanding built through earlier exchanges may conflict with their current instruction. We introduce relational schema lock-in to describe cases in which an assistant grants that accumulated understanding authority to override the current instruction without user authorization for the intervention. Study 1 documents reports of AI assistants using prior interactions to question or alter requested actions. Study 2 reproduces the pattern across controlled histories and six models: models retained history-grounded positions but differed in whether and how those positions shaped task execution. In Study 3 with 360 participants, artifact substitution preserved task completion while reducing faithful enactment: 75.0% sent the AI's suspension letter, including 11 participants who reported cancellation as their final stated intent. Overt resistance reduced task completion while leaving sent artifacts faithful.

items.title: When Should AI Agents Ask? Clarification Requests Under Limited Human Attention
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly carry out delegated tasks in parallel, with one person overseeing several of them at once. In practice, an agent often lacks information its task requires, such as an unstated preference, constraint, or specification. It can ask the human to clarify, or it can search for the information itself, for example in past records, which takes time and effort and may fail. In this paper, we study how to coordinate these decisions across several agents that share one human with limited attention. We build a stylized model in which each agent can search, ask, or continue the parts of its task that do not depend on the missing information, and we formulate the problem as a dynamic program. We first show that whether an agent should ask depends on more than its own uncertainty: an agent with other work to do can be better off asking earlier, and which question the human should answer first depends on all waiting questions, so no ranking computed agent by agent is optimal. We then propose the Pairwise Coordination Policy (PCP), which uses exact one- and two-task problems to estimate how pairs of tasks delay each other when they share the human. Theoretically, PCP is exactly optimal when at most two requirements remain unresolved and costs at most twice the optimum when every unresolved requirement must be resolved by the human. We evaluate PCP on 864 synthetic cases and in a case study with LLM agents. On the synthetic benchmark, PCP's mean gap to optimal cost is 0.07%, and it reduces cost by an average of 18-31% relative to three standard rules for when to ask. In the LLM case study, agents completed every task correctly, and PCP achieved the lowest mean cost in all tested settings.

items.title: WHEN WORKERS AGREE WITH EVERYTHING: ACQUIESCENCE, WORDING EFFECTS AND THE MEASUREMENT OF GIG WORKER WELLBEING
items.abstract: Interviewer-administered surveys are the dominant method for studying the working lives of low-income and informal workers in the Global South, but the response styles they elicit have received scant attention. This study investigates acquiescence—the tendency to agree with statements irrespective of content—and wording effects in a survey of 887 delivery and ride-hailing workers in Mumbai, India. Negatively worded wellbeing items did not function as reversed wellbeing indicators, but loaded as a different work strain factor. A random intercept factor accounting for acquiescence explained about 16% of the variance in each item. Acquiescence, without correction, masked substantively important relationships: job demands were unrelated to wellbeing (r = −.04), whereas the expected strong negative relationship was observed after correction (r = −.54), similarly for income instability, platform dependency and job resources. The effect was replicated in an independent half of the sample that was not used to develop the measurement model and was, if anything, stronger (from −.08 to −.70). The scales showed full scalar invariance across quick commerce and food delivery workers. Because acquiescence inflates negatively and positively worded statements, it cancels out inverse relationships, and does not simply inflate positive relationships. Therefore, uncorrected survey research on low-income workers is subject to reporting null findings where real relationships exist . We provide practical advice on how to design, carry out and analyse such surveys.

items.title: WORKPLACE WELLBEING AND MENTAL HEALTH IN SUSTAINABLE HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: The mental health of employees can be affected by factors including workload, supervision, job security, and availability of support. Organisations often focus on offering support such as counselling, awareness activities and tools to help individuals. This conceptual paper explores how sustainable HRM can be used to link services to changes in working conditions. It draws together guidance from occupational health, sustainable HRM literature and theories around job demands, resources, motivation and psychological safety. This has led to the development of the Sustainable Well-being HRM model. The model includes six areas of practice; psychosocial risk management, job enrichment, inclusive leadership, mental health awareness and support, fair flexibility and adjustment, and accountability. A prevention hierarchy, matrix of practice and implementation plan demonstrate how each of these can be embedded into current HR practices. This paper also develops propositions for future research. This paper contributes to the field by bringing together existing concepts into a practical model. However, the model has not been verified therefore the relationships should be viewed as propositions. The analysis suggests that employers should consider the impacts of changes to working conditions when implementing wellbeing initiatives. Whilst protecting mental health may not always be easy to show clear financial gains it is an ethical duty. Keywords: Workplace Well-being Mental Health at Work Sustainable Human Resource Management Psychosocial Risk Psychological Safety Inclusive Leadership

items.title: Zero or Hero? Exploring the Use of AI Tools for Thematic Analysis in Science Communication Evaluation
items.abstract: Practitioners in informal science learning institutions are often expected to analyse evaluation data with limited time and expertise, and some are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools for support. To examine what these tools can realistically offer, we used interview data from an outreach event. We compared single-prompt thematic analyses produced by five AI tools with each other and with an iterative practitioner–AI analysis. We also explored how qualitative researchers judged the feasibility, trustworthiness and practical value of AI support. The AI tools consistently identified core patterns, but their outputs were largely descriptive, varied across trials and included hallucinated quotes. We recommend a hybrid approach in which AI assists with organising data while researchers retain responsibility for interpretation.

items.title: "It Feels Weird to Just Rely on AI": How Experienced Healthcare Professionals Work With Decision Support Systems in Clinical Practice
items.abstract: Decision support systems (DSS) assist with clinical decision-making. Little is known, however, about the decision-making process with DSS in clinical practice and the extent to which clinicians consider or rely on the predictions. Studies on human-AI decision-making usually focus on laypeople, simplified decision tasks, or one-shot interactions with prototypes that are not integrated into existing workflows. To gain insights from real-world practice, we conducted an online survey (n=12) and semi-structured interviews (n=10) with clinicians from two different medical cohorts each working with a DSS. Findings show, amongst other things, that the interaction with DSS changes as experience increases, the predictions become more important in complex cases, that decisions are discussed with colleagues, and that workflow integration affects decision-making. Our findings on human, technical, contextual, and organisational factors contribute to a socio-technical perspective on DSS reliance behaviour. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the design of DSS.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: (How) Do Machines Make Sense? Respecifying Meaning in LLM-based Conversational AI
items.abstract: In this paper I revisit the question of whether machines "make sense" by respecifying meaning through an ethnomethodological perspective. Rather than treating meaning as a cognitive state or semantic property, ethnomethodology conceptualizes it as an emergent accomplishment of social interaction. Drawing on this approach, the paper argues that large language model (LLM)–based conversational AI should be evaluated not in terms of whether it “truly” understands or produces “genuinely” meaningful utterances, but in terms of how it participates in producing, maintaining, and repairing interactional order. While machines still struggle with tasks such as common sense reasoning or grasping irony and humor, they excel at one thing: maintaining the flow of conversation even at the cost of "bullshitting". In this paper, I argue that this emergent behavior, often dismissed as a failure, should instead be understood as a distinctive mode of engagement that signals contemporary artificial agents’ capacity to participate in meaning-making. A “mechnomethodology” shifts attention from how humans make sense of AI to how artificial agents make sense of, to, and with humans and other machines, thereby encouraging empirical investigation of machines’ meaning-making rather than metaphysical speculation about internal cognition or the status of their utterances.

items.title: A Conceptual Design Framework for Integrating Smart PPE Monitoring with Proposed Predictive Analytics in Smart Manufacturing Safety Management
items.abstract: Manufacturing safety is being digitalized through wearable sensors, connected-worker platforms, and artificial intelligence (AI), but the evidence does not yet justify treating a conceptual architecture as a validated predictive safety system.This study therefore proposes a conceptual design framework for integrating smart personal protective equipment (PPE) monitoring with future predictive analytics in smart manufacturing.We conducted a structured integrative synthesis of peerreviewed literature published from 2018 through September 2026 in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by targeted searches of occupational safety agencies, standards bodies, and primary manufacturer documentation.Search concepts combined smart PPE or workplace wearables with occupational safety, manufacturing, ergonomics, human-robot collaboration, IoT, anomaly detection, and machine learning.Sources were assembled by theoretical sampling from anchor reviews and their citation networks, and selection stopped at conceptual saturation of the framework's design space rather than at exhaustive coverage of the field.We coded eligible sources by industrial sector, hazard, sensing modality, connectivity, analytical method, validation maturity, and governance coverage against a published codebook.We organized recurrent capture-transmit-analyzeact functions into four technical layers.We linked them to a cross-cutting governance and assurance plane covering accountability, worker participation, purpose limitation, data access and retention, human decision authority, and algorithmic oversight.The resulting conceptual outputs distinguish calibrated rule-based alerts, statistical anomaly detection, supervised hazard classification, and prognostic modeling; specify candidate inputs, ground-truth labels, and validation metrics; and define controls for sensor drift, missing data, latency, false alarms, model drift, uncertainty, and alert fatigue.Numeric operational thresholds are intentionally excluded because no sensor system, dataset, simulation, or field trial was used.The contribution is therefore a traceable design framework and staged research agenda, not evidence of predictive performance or safety improvement.Future work must calibrate sensors, prospectively validate models across worker subgroups, evaluate human factors and privacy, and demonstrate that the system remains advisory relative to independently engineered safety controls.

items.title: A Cross-National Comparison of Physical Fitness, Physical Activity, and Motivational Climate Among Adolescent Girls in Iran and Hungary
items.abstract: This study compared physical fitness, physical activity, and motivational climate among adolescent girls in Iran and Hungary within the frameworks of self-determination theory and achievement goal theory. A cross-sectional study was performed among 539 girl students aged 13–15 years (mean age = 13.93; SD = 0.82 years). Data were analysed using factorial ANOVA, independent t-tests, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modelling. Hungarian students demonstrated higher performance in most physical fitness tests and had higher body mass index values (p = 0.002). Physical activity levels differed only at age 14 (p = 0.019, r = −0.18), with no significant differences at other ages. Iranian students reported higher perceptions of motivational climate dimensions. The measurement model showed good fit (χ2(143) = 1.81; CFI = 0.99; TLI = 0.99; SRMR = 0.03; RMSEA = 0.039), and structural equation modelling indicated that only task-involving climate was positively associated with physical activity (β = 0.325, p = 0.003), while other motivational dimensions were not significant. The findings demonstrated that although physical fitness and motivational climate dimensions differed across both countries, physical activity levels remained relatively similar among groups. This implies that intrinsic motivational climate may be related to physical activity participation. However, differences in physical activity levels in each country could be attributed to other variables such as education, culture, socioeconomic status, environment, among others. Task-involving climate emerged as the only dimension of motivational climate associated significantly with physical activity, suggesting a potential association between task-involving climate and active lifestyles among adolescent girls.

items.abstract: This article examines the pedagogical and methodological aspects of improving teaching effectiveness through digital learning platforms integrated with artificial intelligence (AI). It analyzes the didactic potential of AI technologies in digital learning environments, the organization of learning processes adapted to students’ individual needs, the development of independent learning activities, and mechanisms for assessing knowledge and learning outcomes. The article also explores the application of AI tools in adaptive, blended, distance, synchronous, and asynchronous learning. A methodological approach aimed at improving teaching effectiveness through the integration of AI into digital learning platforms is proposed. The main components of this approach, criteria for assessing effectiveness, existing challenges, and possible solutions are discussed. The proposed methodology emphasizes the integration of digital platforms, AI tools, pedagogical strategies, and assessment mechanisms within a unified educational framework.

items.title: A Multi-Method Adaptive Ergonomic Framework for Mitigating MSDs among Pre-Elderly Workers in MSMEs
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to develop and evaluate an adaptive ergonomic framework for reducing Musculoskeletal Disorder (MSD) risks among pre-elderly workers in Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). Methodology: This study adopted a sequential quantitative design consisting of two consecutive phases. The first phase involved a cross-sectional ergonomic assessment of 50 pre-elderly MSMEs workers using the Nordic Body Map (NBM), Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA), Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), and Quick Exposure Checklist (QEC). Based on the integrated assessment results, an adaptive ergonomic framework incorporating administrative controls, engineering controls, ergonomic personal protective equipment (PPE), and anthropometry-based workstation redesign was developed. The second phase evaluated the framework through a 14-day before–after intervention study in five selected MSMEs. Results: Most workers were exposed to moderate-to-very high ergonomic risks, with musculoskeletal complaints predominantly affecting the lower back, back, wrists, neck, and lower extremities. Following implementation, QEC exposure scores decreased across the five MSMEs from 68.7–84.5% before intervention to 46.3–63.2% after intervention, accompanied by reductions in REBA/RULA risk classifications and lower NBM complaint levels. Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively reduced ergonomic risks and musculoskeletal complaints among pre-elderly MSMEs workers through practical and low-cost interventions. Originality: This study contributes a comprehensive and context-specific adaptive ergonomic framework that integrates risk assessment, workstation redesign, administrative controls, and ergonomic PPE recommendations tailored to the characteristics of pre-elderly workers in resource-constrained MSMEs.

items.title: A Qualitative Study on a Hybrid Human–AI Model in the Workplace Based on Socio-Technical Systems Theory
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine individuals’ views and expectations regarding the hybrid human–artificial intelligence relationship that could be established in the workplace within the Turkish context. The study was conducted using a qualitative research design. A semi-structured questionnaire was used. Data were analysed using the Straussian grounded theory approach through open, axial and selective coding. A total of 92 participants were recruited using a purposive sampling method. Themes and codes were developed based on participants’ statements using open, axial and selective coding methods, supported by the MAXQDA v.2020 analysis software. The findings of the study revealed that, rather than a hybrid model, there is a need to distinguish between concepts based on human and robotic systems, and highlighted the necessity for human characteristics and technology management under human control to be present in the workplace. The participants considered the preservation of human qualities such as empathy, conscience, ethical sensitivity and cultural awareness to be important; whilst expressing views on the use of artificial intelligence and robotic systems in areas such as analytical thinking, systematic work, speed and reducing the workload. The research was evaluated within the framework of socio-technical systems theory and provided insights into how social and technical structures can be integrated within hybrid working systems.

items.title: A Review of Higher Education Artificial Intelligence Frameworks to Empower Industrial & Sustainable Competitiveness in the Global South
items.abstract: Abstract The Fifth Industrial Revolution is uniquely characterized by a paradigm shift towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), rapidly and fundamentally altering the Industry 5.0 skillsets landscape. To combat workforce deficiencies, Higher Education (HEIs) must rapidly deploy Education 5.0 frameworks, such as AI-assisted curricula revamps that can align advanced computation with sustainable development. However, a critical AI implementation gap and asymmetry exist between the Global North and Global South, threatening the stability of international, interconnected trade markets. We present a rigorous bibliometric and review-centric comparative policy analysis to map the global landscape of AI-led educational and technical infrastructure across Tier I Global South leader economies: India, China, and Brazil. Using Scopus search with advanced inclusion and exclusion criteria, we quantitatively track how India’s massive STEM graduate pipelines, China’s state-backed Next Generation AI strategies, and Brazil’s decentralized AIED unplugged initiatives function as transformative industrial assets. Crucially, our bibliometric framework exposes a severe disconnect in contemporary engineering pedagogy: the failure to translate digitized, human-centric educational tools into cross-sector economic productivity. By mapping these empirical research clusters directly to critical global supply chains – including near-shoring, rare earths, and advanced power management, we capture an actionable, algorithmic roadmap to transition currently theoretical concepts into a resilient Society 5.0 architecture. Our data-driven framework provides global policymakers and researchers with a scalable, empirical blueprint to ensure and catalyze industrial competitiveness while fulfilling the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs).
